provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General that any error or omission has been made in registering any instrument, whether before or after the commencement of this Ordinance, the Registrar-General shall issue notice in writing in the prescribed form (a) in the case of a deed to the parties thereto; or (b) in the case of a will to the executor or administrator, as the case may be; or (c) in the case of any other instrument to the person who presented it for registration, and order such error or omission to be corrected
provisions.why_relevant: This is the operative correction power. It fixes the first three steps of the procedure: the error must be shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General, who then issues written notice in the prescribed form to the parties to the deed (Deed No. 351), and orders the correction. Registering the sub-divided Lot 3A in the parent folio Vol/Folio A 350/25 is an error or omission made in registering an instrument.
provisions.temporal_note: Subsection (1) was repealed and re-substituted by section 3 of the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act, No. 50 of 1982; the consolidated corpus text is that substituted text and it is the text in force in October 2018. No later amendment in the corpus (Nos. 5 of 1990, 21 of 2013, 32 of 2022, 18 of 2024) touches section 35.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: and order such error or omission to be corrected and the correction shall then be made by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner, but shall not affect any priority accrued before the correction is made
provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the last two steps: after the Registrar-General's order the correction is made by the Registrar concerned (here the Registrar of Lands, Homagama) in the prescribed manner, and it does not disturb any priority that accrued before it. Without this the procedure is incomplete and the effect of the correction on priority is unstated.
provisions.temporal_note: Same 1982 substituted text as PROV-M098-001; in force at the matter reference date of October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Provided that the Registrar-General may with like effect make such an order for the correction of any error or omission made in registering any such instrument if it is proved to his satisfaction by any person interested that by reason of the death or legal incapacity of any person or party to whom notice is required to be issued as aforesaid or for any other sufficient cause whatsoever, such notice cannot be issued.
provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the alternative route where notice to a party to Deed No. 351 cannot be issued. Supporting rather than indispensable, because the facts do not state that any party has died or is incapacitated, but a complete statement of the procedure should note it.
provisions.temporal_note: Same 1982 substituted text; in force at October 2018.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every instrument presented for registration shall be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected by the instrument is situated and in the folio in which 1974] the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or in another folio (whether of the same volume or of another volume) bearing a separate number, opened in continuation thereof, cross reference being entered in the prescribed manner so as to connect the said folios
provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the standard that was breached and so identifies what the error is. It is what makes the registration of the divided Lot 3A in the parent folio of Lot 3 wrong: the sub-divided lot should have been carried to a separate folio opened in continuation, connected by cross reference. Without it the assertion that there is an error in registering has no statutory support.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: A Commissioner or a Deputy Commissioner may exercise, perform or discharge any power, duty or function conferred or imposed on, or assigned to, an Assessor by this Statute.
provisions.why_relevant: Bridges the gap the researcher flagged. Section 48(1) computes duty on the value of the property conveyed and the section 106 definition of value is the open-market price in the opinion of the Assessor, an office section 106 defines as a Provincial Assessor of Revenue. The facts give the opinion of valuation of the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council. Section 104(4) lets a Commissioner discharge any function assigned to an Assessor, so the Commissioner's Rs. 7,500,000 opinion is an opinion within the section 106 definition. Without it the step from the Commissioner's valuation to the statutory base is unsupported.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The question asks for the statutory procedure to correct an error made by the registering officer. Section 35 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance sets that procedure out end to end, from the showing of the error to the Registrar-General through notice in the prescribed form to the parties to the deed, the order to correct, and the correction by the Registrar concerned; section 14 supplies the folio rule that was broken. No judicial authority or Roman-Dutch doctrine is needed to state the steps. The only material outside the statute is the subsidiary prescription of forms and manner under section 49, which is procedural detail rather than a separate source of authority.

legal_issues.issue: Whether registering the divided Lot 3A in Vol/Folio A 350/25, the folio of the parent Lot 3, is an error or omission made in registering an instrument within section 35(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance.
What steps the Registration of Documents Ordinance requires to have that registration corrected, and which officer takes each step.
What effect the correction has on priorities accrued before it, and what happens where notice to a party to Deed No. 351 cannot be issued.

questions.hop_count_basis: Two necessary steps. First, section 14(1) fixes the folio in which an instrument affecting the sub-divided land must be registered, which is what makes the entry in Vol/Folio A 350/25 an error. Second, that error triggers the correction machinery in section 35(1), whose notice, order and correction sequence is the answer. Nothing beyond these two linked provisions is indispensable; the proviso, the prescribed forms and the refusal-appeal route are supporting or background. Verifier: hop count of 2 confirmed; section 14(1) and section 35(1) are the only two indispensable links, and the section 25 definition of 'instrument' for Chapter V is confirmatory rather than a further hop.

enrichment.original_background: Lot 3 of the land called Mahatenna in extent of 30 perches in Plan No. 251 dated 5/7/1999 made by A.Samaranayaka Liscensed Surveyor is registered in the Homagama Land Registry under Vol/Folio A 350/25. The owner, sub divided Lot 3 into 2 lots namely Lots 34 and 3B as depicted in Plan No.255 dated 8/12/2000 made by the same Surveyor. He sold Lot 3A to Dininda Perera by Deed No.351 attested by Gamini Herath, Notary Public. Lot 3A was sold at a price of Rupees 7 million but the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council in his opinion of valuation for stamp duty, values the property at Rupees 7.5 million. Dininda Perera constructed a house on Lot 3A and Leased it out to Nimal Fernando for 2 years on a monthly rental of Rs. 75,000/-, He obtained 1 years rent as an advance to set off against 2nd years rent. When the Lease Agreement was submitted for registration the Land Registry informed that it could not be registered because the sub division of Lot 3A is wrongfully registered in the same folio as the original land (Lot 3) is registered namely in Vol/Folio A 350/25.

gold_answer_draft.issue: By what procedure under the Registration of Documents Ordinance can the wrongful registration of the divided Lot 3A in Vol/Folio A 350/25, the folio of the parent Lot 3, be corrected, so that instruments affecting Lot 3A, including the lease to Nimal Fernando, can be duly registered?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1) requires every instrument to be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land lies and in the folio in which the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or in another folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of it, with cross references entered in the prescribed manner to connect the folios; proviso (a) allows the Registrar, if he thinks fit, to enter an instrument in a new folio with cross references to any previous registration affecting the same land or any part of it. By s.14(2) an instrument is not deemed duly registered unless it is registered in accordance with s.14. Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General that any error or omission has been made in registering any instrument, s.35(1) requires the Registrar-General to issue notice in writing in the prescribed form, in the case of a deed to the parties to it, and to order the error or omission to be corrected; the correction is then made by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner, but does not affect any priority accrued before the correction is made. The proviso to s.35(1) allows the Registrar-General to make the same order on proof by any person interested where, by reason of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, that notice cannot be issued. The form of the notice and the manner of the correction are prescribed by regulation under s.49 and by the forms in the Second Schedule under s.50, and by s.2(6) the Registrar-General may himself exercise a Registrar's powers.
gold_answer_draft.application: Lot 3A is a divided and defined portion of Lot 3, carved out by Plan No. 255 of 8/12/2000 and conveyed to Dininda Perera by Deed No. 351. Under s.14(1) the registration of Deed No. 351 should have been carried to a folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of Vol/Folio A 350/25 and connected to it by cross reference, or under proviso (a) to a new folio with cross references; entering it in the parent folio of Lot 3 itself is therefore not registration in accordance with s.14, and by s.14(2) it is not due registration. That is an error or omission made in registering an instrument for the purposes of s.35(1), and it is the reason the Land Registry says the lease cannot be registered. The procedure is administrative. A person interested, Dininda Perera as proprietor of Lot 3A or the party who presented the lease, applies in writing to the Registrar-General of Lands through the Homagama Land Registry, setting out the error and producing the material that shows it: Deed No. 351, Plan No. 251 and Plan No. 255, and a certified extract of Vol/Folio A 350/25. If the error is shown to the Registrar-General's satisfaction, s.35(1) obliges him to issue notice in writing in the prescribed form; because the instrument concerned is a deed, notice goes to the parties to Deed No. 351, that is the vendor and Dininda Perera, and he orders the error to be corrected. If a party cannot be noticed because of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, the proviso lets the Registrar-General make the order on proof to his satisfaction by any person interested. On that order the Registrar of Lands, Homagama, makes the correction in the prescribed manner, carrying the registration of Lot 3A to a separate folio opened in continuation of, and cross referenced to, Vol/Folio A 350/25. By the closing words of s.35(1) the correction does not affect any priority accrued before it is made, so it cannot prejudice interests already ranked in the old folio. Once the folio is corrected the lease to Nimal Fernando can be presented again for registration in the folio of Lot 3A. If instead the Registrar makes a formal order refusing registration, a separate route exists in s.38(1), an appeal to the Registrar-General within thirty days, but that addresses the refusal and not the folio error.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The error is corrected administratively under the Registration of Documents Ordinance and not by court order. An interested party applies to the Registrar-General of Lands showing the error; on being satisfied, the Registrar-General issues notice in the prescribed form to the parties to Deed No. 351 and orders the correction under s.35(1); the Registrar of Lands, Homagama, then makes the correction in the prescribed manner by carrying the registration of Lot 3A into a separate folio cross referenced to Vol/Folio A 350/25 as s.14(1) requires; and the correction leaves untouched any priority that accrued before it was made. The lease can then be presented for registration in the corrected folio.

answer_claims.claim_text: An instrument affecting land must be registered in the folio in which the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or in another folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of it, with cross references entered in the prescribed manner.
An instrument is not deemed duly registered unless it is registered in accordance with section 14.

Where an error or omission in registering an instrument is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General, he must issue written notice in the prescribed form, in the case of a deed to the parties to the deed, and order the error to be corrected.
The correction is then made by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner and does not affect any priority accrued before the correction is made.

Where notice to a party cannot be issued because of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, the Registrar-General may make the same correction order on proof to his satisfaction by any person interested.
The prescribed form of the notice and the prescribed manner of correction are fixed by regulation and by the forms in the Second Schedule, not by section 35 itself.

Because Lot 3A is a divided portion of Lot 3 depicted in Plan No. 255, the registration of Deed No. 351 belonged in a separate folio opened in continuation of, and cross referenced to, Vol/Folio A 350/25 rather than in that folio itself.
Registering the sub division of Lot 3A in the parent folio Vol/Folio A 350/25 is therefore an error or omission made in registering an instrument for the purposes of section 35(1).

A person interested, such as Dininda Perera or the party who presented the lease, must first apply to the Registrar-General of Lands through the Homagama Land Registry and show the error to his satisfaction, producing Deed No. 351, Plan No. 251, Plan No. 255 and an extract of Vol/Folio A 350/25.
The Registrar-General, if satisfied, issues notice in the prescribed form to the parties to Deed No. 351, namely the vendor and Dininda Perera, and orders the correction.

The Registrar of Lands, Homagama, then carries the registration of Lot 3A into a separate folio cross referenced to Vol/Folio A 350/25, without disturbing priorities accrued before the correction, after which the lease to Nimal Fernando can be presented again for registration.

The correction is obtained administratively under section 35(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, by application to the Registrar-General, notice in the prescribed form to the parties to the deed, an order to correct, and correction by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner, and no court order is required.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: Everything the question turns on is statutory: the charge on an instrument transferring immovable property in the Western Province, the rule that duty is computed on value rather than on the stated price, the definition of value as the open-market price in the opinion of the revenue officer, and who pays. No judicial authority or common-law doctrine is needed. The obstacle is not the kind of authority but its availability: the rate itself is set by subsidiary legislation under section 77 of the Statute, and that rate schedule is not in the frozen corpus, so the arithmetic cannot be completed from a verified provision.

legal_issues.issue: Which enactment charges stamp duty on Deed No. 351, a transfer of immovable property at Homagama in the Western Province.
Whether the duty is computed on the stated price of Rs. 7,000,000 or on the Rs. 7,500,000 opinion of valuation of the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council.
What rate applies to that base, and by whom the duty is payable.

questions.hop_count_basis: Three linked steps. One, section 37 of the Western Province Financial Statute charges duty on an instrument transferring immovable property in the Province at the prescribed rate. Two, section 48(1) fixes the base as the value of the property conveyed rather than the consideration. Three, the definition of value in section 106 makes that base the open-market price in the opinion of the revenue officer, which is what lets Rs. 7,500,000 displace Rs. 7,000,000. A fourth step, the prescribed rate, is required to finish the calculation but has no provision in the corpus. Verifier: raised from three to four. Section 104(4) of the Statute is a further indispensable link, because the section 106 definition of value speaks of the opinion of the Assessor while the facts give the opinion of the Commissioner of Revenue; without section 104(4) the Rs. 7,500,000 figure does not reach the statutory base.

enrichment.original_background: Lot 3 of the land called Mahatenna in extent of 30 perches in Plan No. 251 dated 5/7/1999 made by A.Samaranayaka Liscensed Surveyor is registered in the Homagama Land Registry under Vol/Folio A 350/25. The owner, sub divided Lot 3 into 2 lots namely Lots 34 and 3B as depicted in Plan No.255 dated 8/12/2000 made by the same Surveyor. He sold Lot 3A to Dininda Perera by Deed No.351 attested by Gamini Herath, Notary Public. Lot 3A was sold at a price of Rupees 7 million but the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council in his opinion of valuation for stamp duty, values the property at Rupees 7.5 million. Dininda Perera constructed a house on Lot 3A and Leased it out to Nimal Fernando for 2 years on a monthly rental of Rs. 75,000/-, He obtained 1 years rent as an advance to set off against 2nd years rent. When the Lease Agreement was submitted for registration the Land Registry informed that it could not be registered because the sub division of Lot 3A is wrongfully registered in the same folio as the original land (Lot 3) is registered namely in Vol/Folio A 350/25.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What stamp duty is payable on Deed No. 351, by which Lot 3A at Homagama was transferred to Dininda Perera, where the stated price is Rs. 7,000,000 but the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council has given an opinion of valuation of Rs. 7,500,000?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Western Province Financial Statute s.37 charges stamp duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, and allows different rates for different classes of instrument. By s.48(1) the duty with which a conveyancing instrument is chargeable is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration expressed in it. Section 106 defines value, for property other than immovable property that is gifted, as the price which in the opinion of the Assessor the property would have fetched in the open market on the relevant date; the same section defines Commissioner as the Provincial Commissioner of Revenue and Assessor as a Provincial Assessor of Revenue. By s.51(a) the duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee unless there is an agreement to the contrary, and by s.40(1) it is payable before or at the time of execution. The rate is not stated in the Statute: s.37 refers to the prescribed rate and s.77(1) empowers the Minister to make regulations on any matter the Statute requires to be prescribed. Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 expressly leaves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property outside the provisions of that Act that displace the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982.
gold_answer_draft.application: Lot 3A lies at Homagama and is registered in the Homagama Land Registry, so the land transferred by Deed No. 351 is immovable property situated in the Western Province and the deed is charged under s.37. Under s.48(1) the base of the charge is the value of Lot 3A, and under the s.106 definition that value is the open-market price in the opinion of the revenue officer. The Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council has given an opinion of valuation of Rs. 7,500,000, which exceeds the Rs. 7,000,000 at which the lot was sold. The duty is therefore computed on Rs. 7,500,000 and not on the price the parties recorded, and by s.51(a) it falls on Dininda Perera as grantee unless the deed provides otherwise. The remaining element, the rate to be applied to Rs. 7,500,000, is set by regulation under s.77(1) and is not reproduced in any provision available here, so the rupee figure cannot be stated on verified authority. The verifier should also confirm whether the opinion of a Commissioner of Revenue is an opinion of the Assessor for the purposes of the s.106 definition, since that definition names the Assessor.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Deed No. 351 is chargeable with stamp duty under s.37 of the Western Province Financial Statute, computed under s.48(1) on the value of Lot 3A, which by the s.106 definition is the Rs. 7,500,000 open-market valuation rather than the Rs. 7,000,000 price, and payable by Dininda Perera as grantee under s.51(a). The final arithmetic cannot be given: the prescribed rate is fixed by regulation under s.77(1) and no rate schedule exists in the corpus, so this question is recorded as blocked for missing authority rather than answered with a figure.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty at the prescribed rate is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument, the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration stated.
Value means the price which, in the opinion of the revenue officer, the property would have fetched in the open market on the relevant date.
Duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee unless there is an agreement to the contrary, and is payable before or at the time of execution.
The rate is not fixed by the Statute itself; section 37 charges duty at the prescribed rate and the Minister prescribes that rate by regulation.
Transfers of immovable property are carved out of the displacing provisions of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, so the deed is not stamped under that Act.
Lot 3A, registered in the Homagama Land Registry, is immovable property situated in the Western Province, so Deed No. 351 is charged under section 37.
The base of the charge is Rs. 7,500,000, the Commissioner of Revenue's opinion of valuation, and not the Rs. 7,000,000 price at which Lot 3A was sold.
The duty falls on Dininda Perera as grantee under Deed No. 351, absent an agreement to the contrary.

The rate to be applied to Rs. 7,500,000 sits in regulations made under section 77(1) and no such rate schedule is available in the corpus, so the rupee amount cannot be computed on verified authority.
Deed No. 351 is chargeable with provincial stamp duty computed on a value of Rs. 7,500,000 and payable by the grantee, but the calculation is left open for want of the prescribed rate.

questions.block_reason: The question asks for a calculation. Section 37 of the Western Province Financial Statute charges the duty at the prescribed rate and section 77(1) leaves that rate to regulations made by the Minister and published in the Gazette. No rate schedule or Order fixing the ad valorem rate for transfers of immovable property in the Western Province as at October 2018 is present in the frozen corpus, and the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 likewise charges duty at the prescribed rate in section 2 without stating one. The base of the calculation (Rs. 7,500,000) and the payer are established on statutory authority, but the rupee figure cannot be produced without inventing a rate, so the question is recorded as blocked rather than answered. Verifier: the block is confirmed. grep of 6-1990, 43-1982 and 12-2006 for 'per centum' and 'hundred thousand' returns only penalty and refund percentages, and no rate order is in the corpus. The base of Rs. 7,500,000 is now fully supported following the addition of PROV-M098-901 (section 104(4)), so the only missing element is the rate.
